title: Lists
explain: A list holds an ordered collection of items in square brackets. You can add with `append`, read by index starting at 0, and slice with `[start:stop]`. Lists are mutable, so changing one changes it everywhere it is referenced.
code:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
fruits.append("mango")
print(fruits[0])        # apple
print(fruits[-1])       # mango
print(fruits[1:3])      # ['banana', 'cherry']
fruits.remove("banana")
print(len(fruits), fruits)

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a            # same list, not a copy
b.append(4)
print(a)         # [1, 2, 3, 4]
exercise: Make a list of five numbers, then print the largest, the smallest and the list sorted from high to low without changing the original.
tip: Writing `b = a` does not copy a list. Use `b = a.copy()` or `list(a)` when you need an independent copy.
